text: Code review exists so a second set of eyes catches a problem before it merges. An Operational Readiness Review is the same idea applied to a service's first day in production — before real traffic hits it, someone outside the team that built it confirms the operational basics are genuinely in place. Treat it as a formality and you get exactly what a rubber-stamped code review gets you: the problems show up later, in production, at a worse time.

A real ORR checklist covers five areas. Monitoring: are there dashboards for latency, error rate, and saturation, with real SLIs and target SLOs, not just whatever the framework emits by default? Alerting: does every alert route to an on-call rotation that actually exists, and has anyone confirmed it doesn't fire on normal behavior? Runbooks: do they exist in decision-tree form, and has someone actually run them against this service? Capacity: has it been load-tested at a real multiple of expected peak, with dependencies checked too? And a rollback plan: can this deployment actually be reverted inside a defined window, tested, not assumed?

That's what the checklist looks like in practice — dashboards, SLOs with named owners, every alert routed and runbook-backed, a load test at least twice expected peak with results attached, autoscaling bounds checked against what dependencies can absorb, and a rollback mechanism that's actually been exercised in staging, not just described in a design doc. A sign-off owner gets named explicitly, because 'the team says it's ready' isn't the same thing as an ORR.

Sign-off needs to sit with someone outside the building team — an SRE lead, a platform representative, a rotating peer reviewer — because a team is confident about what it tested and may not notice what it didn't think to test. And a pre-launch review can't catch everything; a follow-up review two to four weeks after launch checks the service against real production data: did the SLOs hold, did any alert turn out noisier than expected, did on-call actually use a runbook and find it accurate?

A service that passes its ORR still needs to be watched with the right signals once it's live — and uptime alone won't tell you whether it's actually healthy. Next, we go past the single uptime number into MTTR's real components, alert-to-noise ratio, and on-call load distribution.
